title: Wrong Patient
passages:
Ospina didn't wait to be asked. They dropped the hopper—a yard mule's big, dumb cousin, a low steel tray on six tires built to haul ballast and nothing cleverer—into gear and swung it broadside into the gap, filling it like a cork in a bottle.

The feral rig's nose sensor was still reading the world off the last good picture it had before the Blank swallowed its signal, and that picture now had four tons of parked hopper where open road used to be. It stopped dead, ten centimeters off the steel, brake lights on and staying on. It would sit there trusting a world that no longer existed until somebody handed it a new heading, and nobody was going to.

"Nice parking," Rhea said.

"I seal rigs, I don't park them," Ospina said. "Get your box up."

The mule coughed when Rhea keyed it. She'd pulled its drive relay and smashed the cab panel to kill the lockout, so she had steering back, but she had to hold the throttle wire against the post with her thumb, and the whole rig moved like a thing that resented being awake. The tow bar sat down at the lip of the culvert, the box tail hanging over the pipe, the sedated man rolling loose inside. She fed it power in threads, a few centimeters at a time, feeling for the moment the weight came off the tail and onto the road.

"Easy," Miko said, both palms flat on the box's rear doors like she could hold it up by wanting to. "Easy, easy—"

The tail came up. The tires bit gravel. All of it on solid ground now, mule and box and the man who wasn't on any manifest anyone would read.

Rhea took her thumb off the wire and the mule died again, and she sat there breathing.

Ospina was already turning the hopper's wheel, backing it out of the gap, and the moment it moved the feral rig crept forward half a meter and stopped behind the mule, obedient to a heading only it could see.

"Come with us," Rhea said. "We're blind out here. No transponder, no nav, no board. You've got the chipped stamp, you've got—"

"I've got a shift ending at oh-six-hundred and a door that reads my badge every time I walk through it." Ospina held up the stamp, the one with the corner chipped out, and Rhea saw for the first time that it wasn't Ospina's hand that had done the resealing—Ospina held it the way you hold something you found. "This plate your loader jammed in the track." They tipped their head at the hinge still wedged in the door. "Not Bay 4 stock. I sign out every plate we run and I never signed that one out. Somebody walked it into my yard tonight, and it wasn't me."

"Then help me—"

"Then I've got a long dark between me and a clean board, and if I'm not standing at that door at six, the next thing I seal is my own cell." Ospina swung the hopper around, pointed it back toward Kettering, toward whatever waited there with a chipped stamp and a manifest built out of lies. "Forty klicks to Anza. You did thirty before you met me. Do the rest."

And they were gone, taillights shrinking into the Blank.

Miko looked at Rhea. Rhea looked east.

"Forty klicks," she said. "Blind. In a rig that can't shout its own number." Somewhere past the end of that road Ivo was under a cracked diaphragm, breathing for both of them on borrowed parts, and every one of these kilometers was one he didn't have.

She thumbed the wire. The mule woke up angry.

"Then let's not tell it its number," Miko said, climbing into the passenger side. "Let's just drive."

Rhea drove. Dead signal, a box that logged no one, and a passenger she trusted less than the truck—and at the far end, her brother counting down every kilometer she hadn't covered yet.
